{"problem": {"theorem": "2. Show that there are infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(m, n)$ such that

$$
\frac{m+1}{n}+\frac{n+1}{m}
$$
is a positive integer.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "british_mo", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "target": {"node_id": "n10", "version": 1}, "target_node": {"text": "Because the recurrences (6) make \((t_{k},y_{k})\) – and therefore
\((m_{k},n_{k})\) – grow strictly, the pairs \((m_{k},n_{k})\)
are all distinct.  Thus we have produced infinitely many positive integral
pairs with integral value \(4\).", "claim": "Strict growth of the constructed sequence is invoked to show that its positive-integer pairs are distinct and infinite in number.", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n6", "n7", "n8", "n9"], "goal_refs": []}, "closed_predecessors": [{"node_id": "n1", "version": 1, "claim": "The proof defines S(m,n) and proposes constructing infinitely many positive-integer pairs for which S(m,n)=4.", "text": "Let  

\[
S(m,n)=\frac{m+1}{n}+\frac{n+1}{m}\qquad (m ,n\in \Bbb Z_{>0}).
\]

We shall show that there are infinitely many couples \((m,n)\) with \(S(m,n)\in \Bbb Z\).
It is enough to exhibit infinitely many solutions for a single integral value of
\(S(m,n)\); we choose the value \(4\).", "scope": [], "depends_on": []}, {"node_id": "n2", "version": 1, "claim": "The condition S(m,n)=4 is rewritten as the Diophantine equation m²+n²+m+n−4mn=0.", "text": "--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Reducing the problem to a Diophantine equation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Putting \(S(m,n)=4\) and multiplying by \(mn\) gives  

\[
m(m+1)+n(n+1)=4mn\Longrightarrow
 m^{2}+n^{2}+m+n-4mn=0. \tag{1}
\]", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n1"]}, {"node_id": "n3", "version": 1, "claim": "Equation (1) is viewed as a quadratic in m, whose discriminant condition is t²=12n²−12n+1.", "text": "Regard (1) as a quadratic in \(m\):

\[
m^{2}+(1-4n)m+(n^{2}+n)=0.  \tag{2}
\]

For (2) to possess an integral root \(m\) its discriminant must be a perfect
square:

\[
\Delta=(1-4n)^{2}-4(n^{2}+n)=12n^{2}-12n+1=t^{2}  \tag{3}
\]

for some integer \(t>0\).
Equation (3) is still quadratic; we transform it into a classical Pell type
equation.", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n2"]}, {"node_id": "n4", "version": 1, "claim": "The substitution y=2n−1 transforms the discriminant equation into t²−3y²=−2, with y positive and odd.", "text": "--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A Pell equation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put  

\[
y=2n-1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad n=\frac{y+1}{2}\quad (y\ {\rm odd}>0).
\]

Substituting \(n=(y+1)/2\) in (3):

\[
t^{2}=12\Bigl(\frac{y+1}{2}\Bigr)^{2}-12\Bigl(\frac{y+1}{2}\Bigr)+1
      =3y^{2}-2. 
\]

Hence we must solve  

\[
t^{2}-3y^{2}=-2. \tag{4}
\]", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n3"]}, {"node_id": "n5", "version": 1, "claim": "A norm-multiplication construction combines the solution 1+√3 of norm −2 with powers of 2+√3 of norm 1.", "text": "--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Infinitely many solutions of \(x^{2}-3y^{2}=-2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Equation (4) is a Pell equation with parameter \(d=3\) and right–hand side
\(-2\).  It has the small positive solution \((t_{0},y_{0})=(1,1)\) because
\(1^{2}-3\cdot1^{2}=-2\).

Let \((a,b)=(2,1)\) be the fundamental solution of
\(x^{2}-3y^{2}=1\) (since \(2^{2}-3\cdot1^{2}=1\)).
Because the norm (the left–hand side) is multiplicative,

\[
(t+y\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)^k,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,
\]

always has norm \(-2\) when \((t,y)\) has norm \(-2\).", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n4"]}, {"node_id": "n6", "version": 1, "claim": "The Pell construction defines a recurrence for positive solutions (t_k,y_k) and asserts that every y_k is odd.", "text": "Writing  

\[
(t_{k}+y_{k}\sqrt3)=(1+\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)^k\qquad(k\ge 0) \tag{5}
\]

gives an infinite sequence of solutions \((t_{k},y_{k})\) of (4).
Explicitly (multiplying out (5))

\[
t_{k+1}=2t_{k}+3y_{k},\qquad
y_{k+1}=t_{k}+2y_{k},\qquad (t_{0},y_{0})=(1,1). \tag{6}
\]

Since \(y_{0}=1\) is odd and the recurrence (6) preserves oddness,
every \(y_{k}\,(k\ge 0)\) is odd and positive.", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n5"]}, {"node_id": "n7", "version": 1, "claim": "Each Pell solution defines a positive integer n_k and two stated roots of the quadratic equation for m.", "text": "--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  From \((t_{k},y_{k})\) to \((m_{k},n_{k})\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Set  

\[
n_{k}=\frac{y_{k}+1}{2}\qquad(k\ge 0),
\]
so \(n_{k}\in\Bbb Z_{>0}\).
Because \(t_{k}^{2}=12n_{k}^{2}-12n_{k}+1\), the discriminant in (2) is
\(t_{k}^{2}\), hence (2) has two integer roots

\[
m=\frac{4n_{k}-1\pm t_{k}}{2}. \tag{7}
\]", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n3", "n4", "n6"]}, {"node_id": "n8", "version": 1, "claim": "An inequality is used to establish positivity of the roots, and the larger root is designated m_k.", "text": "To check that each choice is positive note that

\[
4n_{k}-1=2y_{k}+1>t_{k}\quad
(\text{because }(2y_{k}+1)^{2}-t_{k}^{2}
 =(y_{k}+1)(y_{k}+3)>0),
\]

so both numerators in (7) are positive; consequently both roots are
positive integers.
Choose the larger root and denote it \(m_{k}\) (the smaller root gives the
symmetric solution \((n_{k},m_{k})\)).", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n4", "n6", "n7"]}, {"node_id": "n9", "version": 1, "claim": "Every constructed positive-integer pair is asserted to satisfy equation (1), so the required expression equals 4.", "text": "--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Verification
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For every \(k\ge 0\) the pair \((m_{k},n_{k})\) constructed above satisfies
(1), hence

\[
\frac{m_{k}+1}{n_{k}}+\frac{n_{k}+1}{m_{k}}=4\in\Bbb Z.
\]", "scope": [], "depends_on": ["n2", "n7", "n8"]}], "counterexample_search": true, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "ring_quotient_ideal", "name": "Quotient ring criterion", "statement": "If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.", "conditions": ["I is a two-sided ideal of R"], "conclusion": "R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.", "rule_digest": "5c419f063bbc02eba57c0943d5ecce5f2e4c1b370cbb5ad6d69c2e08c3b21835", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}]}
